title: Class 11 Chemistry — Fundamental Principles of Organic Chemistry Study Guide
notes: Choose the longest parent chain containing the principal functional group and maximum multiple bonds. Number to give the senior functional group the lowest locant, then unsaturation and substituents by priority. Name substituents with locants, use di-/tri- for repeats, alphabetize substituent names ignoring multiplicative prefixes, then combine parent, unsaturation and suffix. Check that the name describes one unambiguous structure.

Lassaigne's sodium fusion converts covalently bonded nitrogen, sulfur and halogens into water-soluble ionic salts. Appropriate tests can detect nitrogen (Prussian blue after iron salts and acid), sulfur and halides (silver halide precipitates after acidification with nitric acid). Incomplete fusion and interfering ions can give false results. Sodium and reagents make this a supervised laboratory procedure, never a home experiment.

Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity or spatial arrangement. Structural isomerism includes chain, position, functional-group, metameric and tautomeric forms. Geometrical isomerism requires restricted rotation and, for an alkene, two different substituents on each double-bond carbon. Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of chiral molecules. d/l indicates optical rotation direction, not R/S configuration or D/L biochemical notation.

Homolytic fission divides a bond pair equally and makes radicals. Heterolytic fission gives both bonding electrons to one atom and makes ions. An electrophile accepts an electron pair; a nucleophile donates an electron pair; a free radical has an unpaired electron. Use full-headed curved arrows for electron pairs and fish-hook arrows for single electrons.

The inductive effect is sigma-bond polarization transmitted through a chain and weakens with distance. Groups may show +I electron release or −I withdrawal. Resonance describes electron delocalization through conjugation; +R groups donate electron density and −R groups withdraw it. Resonance contributors are bookkeeping structures for a hybrid: do not move atoms, and preserve total charge and electron count.
keyPoints: Select parent chain and numbering by IUPAC priority, then verify the complete structure.
Lassaigne's test detects selected elements after conversion into ions; it requires safe lab controls.
Cis/trans alkene isomerism needs restricted rotation and different groups on both alkene carbons.
d/l optical rotation is distinct from R/S configuration and D/L notation.
Homolysis produces radicals; heterolysis produces ions.
Inductive effects transmit through sigma bonds; resonance requires conjugation and delocalized electrons.
practiceQuestions: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ and CH₃CH₂CHO by IUPAC rules.
Draw structural isomers of C₄H₁₀ and classify their isomerism.
Explain why 2-butene can show geometrical isomerism.
Distinguish heterolytic from homolytic cleavage of a C–Br bond.
Compare inductive and resonance effects, including how each is transmitted.
summary: Solve organic problems by naming structures correctly, classifying isomerism and tracking electron movement. Keep connectivity, stereochemistry, bond fission and electronic effects distinct.
